claims.text: Rapid melt-spinning at cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s yields an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy.
The rapidly quenched alloy is prone to primary crystallization during conventional reheating.
The proposed intervention is a single high-heating-rate flash reheating step with minimal dwell time immediately after rapid solidification.
Flash reheating will increase amorphous retention in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Flash reheating will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous alloy.
A short flash pulse minimizes the time available for primary crystalline nuclei to grow.
The flash pulse restricts effective diffusion and atomic rearrangement relative to slower reheating.
Restricted diffusion suppresses nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
The flash pulse can relax internal stresses in the amorphous alloy without allowing substantial crystallization.
The flash pulse can improve short-range order in the amorphous alloy without allowing substantial crystallization.
Flash-treated samples will retain more amorphous material during subsequent thermal cycling than conventionally reheated or more slowly cooled samples.
Flash-treated samples will exhibit a delayed crystallization exotherm in DSC.
Flash-treated samples will exhibit a reduced crystallization exotherm in DSC.
Flash-treated samples will show fewer or no XRD peaks from primary crystalline phases.
Slow cooling produces an extensive, complex crystalline microstructure in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The crystalline products formed under slow cooling are specifically primary non-eutectic phases.
Standard reheating produces a multistep crystallization sequence in this alloy.
The FCC crystallization onset under accelerated cooling is approximately 1341 K.
Excessive peak temperature, prolonged dwell time, or insufficient heating rate may cause renewed nucleation and unwanted crystallization.
